claims.text: Retention of structural and chemical stability in initially single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by the balance between mixing enthalpy and kinetically limited atomic diffusion.
Equiatomic mixing can provide entropic stabilization against phase separation.
Lattice strain from multielement mixing can create significant atomic-diffusion barriers.
High diffusion barriers can prevent substantial phase-separating atomic rearrangement even near 1923 K.
Defect density mediates effective diffusion barriers and therefore the onset of segregation or phase separation.
Slow atomic mobility in a strained lattice results from high diffusion activation energy.
Nanoparticles combining strongly negative mixing enthalpies with high diffusion barriers will remain single-phase and chemically homogeneous throughout 473–1923 K.
Compositions with less favorable mixing or lower diffusion barriers will exhibit phase separation, grain growth, or chemical segregation at higher temperatures.
Using an inert or controlled reductive atmosphere minimizes oxidation during thermal testing.
Periodic temperature cycling represents service conditions relevant to catalytic and thermoelectric applications.
Nanoparticle size, surface state, and minor compositional deviations can alter the quantitative effects of mixing enthalpy and kinetic hindrance.
Oxidation or other degradation processes can precede and obscure diffusion-controlled phase separation.
Changing composition slightly can reduce diffusion barriers while retaining a similar overall multimetal composition.
In situ high-temperature XRD, TEM, and elemental mapping can detect phase separation, secondary phases, grain growth, and chemical segregation.
Phase separation or loss of the single-phase structure in the nominally favorable high-barrier material would falsify the proposed kinetic-hindrance explanation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says diffusion barriers suppress the thermodynamic drive for phase separation, whereas the mechanism correctly treats diffusion barriers as kinetic impediments distinct from thermodynamic forces. A kinetic barrier can slow access to phase-separated states but does not itself remove the thermodynamic driving force.
